title: Level a builder's automatic level on its three foot screws
instruction: Level the instrument so its circular bubble is centred in the ring.
context: Every elevation shot on a construction site starts the same way: before a staff can be read, the builder's automatic level is levelled on its three foot screws until its circular bubble is centred, which brings the line of sight within the compensator's working range (about 15'). Construction laborers, carpenters and surveying technicians do it at every setup, many times a day, to carry heights for footings, slabs, forms and drainage falls (O*NET 47-2061, 47-2031, 17-3031; the makers' manuals and surveying texts make it the first step of a setup). The difficulty is robotic: three fine-thread knobs that each tilt the whole instrument, turned by gripping and rotating the wrist with regrips inside its range; a telescope to swing clear; and a real-size bubble that must be looked at closely to be read. Any correct way of centring it counts. Unlike the board's levelling tasks, which move ballast or a support, only the instrument's own screws can level it.
setup: Station table, fixed layout (object_jitter=0 is required); world frame in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x away from the robot, y to its left, z up from the table top. Every part is built by the task file from primitives; there are no third-party assets. A fixed steel column (5 cm across, 4 cm tall) stands at x 26, y 0 with a flat aluminium tripod head on it (18 cm across, 2 cm thick); the levelling base's grey steel plate (22.4 cm across, 6 mm thick) is fixed on the head, its top 6.6 cm above the table. The instrument, a builder's automatic level of 1.6 kg in all, stands on the plate on three foot screws on a circle 10 cm in radius: one toward the robot (x 16, y 0) and two at the front (x 31, y 8.66 and -8.66). The circle and plate are enlarged from a real instrument's (whose foot screws are closer together; exact values unverified) so the gripper's palm clears the telescope. Each foot screw is a black knurled plastic knob (3 cm across, 1.2 cm tall, 15 g) on top of one of the base's three cast-aluminium arms (1.8 cm wide), turning a steel M8 x 1 screw (1 mm per turn, 4 mm of travel either way; clockwise seen from above lowers the screw and lifts that corner) whose rounded steel tip (8 mm across) stands on the plate; a spring-steel washer (2.4 cm across) between each arm and its knob gives the thread its friction. The base is a white painted cast-aluminium body (10 cm across, 4.2 cm tall, 0.70 kg) held down on its screws by a central spring (20 N). On it, turning freely about the vertical axis, is the white painted aluminium telescope (0.85 kg): a housing 10.4 cm across and 2 cm tall with two black plastic horizontal-drive knobs (1.6 cm across, 8 mm thick, look-only) on its sides, a short standard, and a tube 4.6 cm across and 20 cm long, its axis 12 cm above the plate, a black plastic gunsight (4 cm long, 8 mm tall, look-only) on top, with a grey plastic sunshade (5.2 cm across, 3 cm long) over the objective lens at the far end, a black rubber eyecup on the eyepiece (3.4 cm across, 4 cm long) at the near end and a black plastic focusing knob (1.8 cm across, 1.2 cm thick, look-only) on the right. It starts pointing away from the robot, its eyepiece over the back screw. A circular level sits on an aluminium bracket on the housing's left side toward the eyepiece, its centre 5.8 cm from the axis: a glass window 2.8 cm across over yellow-green liquid, a black ring 1 cm across (0.8 mm line) at its centre and a bubble 8 mm across that moves 2 mm for each 8' of tilt toward the high side. At the start the screws are set for a tilt of 24.0' toward 150 degrees from x; the threads give a little under the weight, and the instrument settles tilted 24.4' toward the back-left (148 degrees), between the screws' lines: the bubble's centre is 6.1 mm from the ring's (5.2 mm toward the robot, 3.2 mm to its left).
scoring: Scored at the end, from the tilt of the base (the angle between its vertical axis and the vertical; the bubble moves 2 mm per 8'). 0 if any screw's tip stands more than 0.05 mm above the base plate (the instrument held up rather than standing on its own screws) or more than 0.05 mm into it (pushed down), or the base is tilted more than 2 degrees. Otherwise: 1.0 if the bubble is in the ring (tilt 4' or less, its centre within 1 mm of the ring's) with every tip on the plate, the base still (under 5 mm/s and 0.02 rad/s) and no knob being turned, held for 1 s, which ends the trial; 0.75 if the bubble is in the ring at the end but that has not held for 1 s; 0.5 if the tilt is 8' or less (the bubble touching the ring); 0.25 if it is 15' or less (within the compensator's working range); else 0. Doing nothing (24.4') scores 0, and no single knob can level it (the best leaves 11.5': 0.25). Any way of levelling counts. Nothing scores unless every part and joint of the instrument was built as specified, each screw stands where its knob's turns put it, and every reading is finite.
reset_notes: Fixed layout (object_jitter=0). Set each trial up from level by knob turns, seen from above: the back knob 218 degrees clockwise (its screw 0.605 mm out) and the front-right 218 degrees counter-clockwise (0.605 mm in), the front-left left at level, with the telescope pointing away from the robot.
fidelity: Rigid bodies on PhysX joints, real mass. Each knob turns on a hinge; its screw slides on a stiff sprung joint whose set point follows the knob's turn at 1 mm per turn, set every control step; a spring washer gives the thread's holding friction. The bubble is the top of a damped pendulum hung from the vial's centre of curvature (2 mm per 8'). The screw circle is enlarged for the gripper's palm. No optics or compensator; a fixed column stands in for the tripod.
